medium: Pencil on a spiral-bound sketchbook page; the heading in a darker, finer line
provenance: Drawn by Larry from memory on 2026-09-12, during the sitting in which he commented on the camp, flight-line and mountain photographs that day. He offered to draw it; his son did not ask. His son calls it the flight line and the airport. His son scanned the sheet flat with a phone the same afternoon (a one-page PDF, Scan_20260912_150027 Ton Son Nhut Airport.pdf, 15:00, kept in the archive as it arrived; the filename is his son’s) and sent it to the archive; the sheet stays with the family. The image shown is the page taken out of the PDF without re-encoding. The heading is drawn in a darker, finer line than the pencil labels, and his son confirms that Larry wrote it. That evening his son added, from memory, a report of part of what Larry said while drawing (a paraphrase recollection, held from the site until he has been asked about it himself). Not recorded: whether he was looking at any photograph while he drew, most of the order in which he drew, and anything else he said as he drew.
title: The flight line
description: A plan drawn on a sketchbook page, shown with the spiral binding along the top. Near the top, the word RUNWAY is written above a long horizontal line that runs across most of the page. Below it, in a darker and finer line than the rest of the sheet, a heading of several words runs across the upper centre; it is not transcribed because one of its letters cannot be read with confidence. Below the heading are several short, faint horizontal strokes, and at the far left, under RUNWAY, a short diagonal stroke and a small hooked mark. At the left of the page, standing on a second long line that crosses the page to its right edge, are three small drawings, each with writing above it. The left-hand one is a small rounded shape with long strokes crossing over it, under 007. The middle one is a high-winged aeroplane with a propeller and wheels, under a word that is not transcribed because one of its letters cannot be read with confidence. The right-hand one is a smaller cross-shaped aeroplane under L19. At the right edge, above the second line, a vertical line is crossed by five short horizontal strokes, with a small loop at its top and faint marks between the strokes. Below the second line, two long vertical lines run close together down the page a little right of centre. Left of them is a box with two lines of writing, not transcribed because letters in both lines cannot be read with confidence. Right of them is a large box labelled HANGER, with a second line of writing below it that is left out whole because one of its letters cannot be read with confidence. At the bottom, left of the vertical lines, is a box with two lines of writing, left out whole for the same reason. At the bottom right is a small box labelled MOVIE’S. Nothing on the sheet indicates scale or compass direction.
researchNotes: Drawn the day he placed the flight line in words at the photographs: “At the flight line probably 3 blocks away. There was a Beaver airplane” (VN-0012), “Just taking off on the flight line heading to Nui Ba Den” (VN-0016), and “this is the Flight Line” (VN-0020). The heading is withheld whole for one letter; its legible words, and the candidate readings of the other withheld inscriptions, are in research/drawings/README.md and are not named in this record (2026-09-14: descriptions no longer name partial readings of withheld inscriptions). Whatever it says, a heading names the airfield as he remembers it and is not evidence of where it was; the identification with Tân Sơn Nhứt stays a hypothesis on the place record. L-19 was the Army’s designation for the Cessna Bird Dog until 1962, when it became the O-1; on the sheet L19 is written above a drawing of an aeroplane. The record first described the left-hand drawing on the flight line as a crossed-out aeroplane; that was an interpretation, and the description now gives only the strokes. Why 007 above it is transcribed (the characters could be zeros or letters O) rests on his son's report of what Larry said while drawing, which is held from the site because it answers a question still to be put to him (2026-09-12-drawing-rosethorn-007.json; research/drawings/README.md). The untranscribed boxes, the ladder-like mark at the right edge, and the two close vertical lines are not interpreted here; they are his to explain. The sheet gives no distances, so it does not bear on where his hooch stood relative to the flight line.
